notes:
1. Tamil Nadu Health System — Overall Character

  • Tamil Nadu has developed a comparatively extensive public-health system combining preventive care, primary care, hospitals, medical education, emergency services, insurance and community-based programmes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Health Model → Prevention + Primary Care + Referral + Hospital Care + Financial Protection

2. Changing Health-Care Approach

Tamil Nadu's system has gradually moved from a mainly hospital-centred model towards:

  • Disease prevention.
  • Community screening.
  • Maternal-child health.
  • Emergency care.
  • NCD management.
  • Digital health.
  • Continuous care.

3. Referral-Care Chain

The broad public-health pathway is:

Prevention

→ Primary Care

→ Referral

→ Secondary Care

→ Tertiary Care

📌 Must-Memorise

Each Level Has a Distinct Function

4. Public Health Beyond Treatment

Tamil Nadu's health system also performs:

  • Immunisation.
  • Disease surveillance.
  • Family welfare.
  • Health education.
  • Birth and death registration.
  • Community screening.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Health System ≠ Hospital Treatment Alone

5. Health and Family Welfare Department

The Health and Family Welfare Department coordinates multiple specialised institutions responsible for different parts of the State health system.

6. Major Health Institutions

Important institutions include:

  • Directorate of Public Health and Preventive Medicine.
  • Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services.
  • Directorate of Medical Education and Research.
  • Directorate of Family Welfare.
  • Directorate of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy.
  • National Health Mission Tamil Nadu.
  • Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation.
  • Tamil Nadu Health Systems Project.
  • Tamil Nadu State AIDS Control Society.
  • Medical Services Recruitment Board.

7. Directorate of Public Health and Preventive Medicine

Its principal responsibilities include:

  • Primary health care.
  • Preventive medicine.
  • Disease surveillance.
  • Maternal and child health.
  • Immunisation.
  • Vital statistics.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPH → Prevention + Primary Care + Surveillance

8. Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services

  • It manages major non-teaching government hospitals.
  • These include district, taluk and non-taluk institutions.
📌 Must-Memorise

DMRHS → Secondary-Level Non-Teaching Government Hospitals

9. Directorate of Medical Education and Research

It performs two major functions:

  • Medical and paramedical education.
  • Administration of major teaching hospitals and tertiary care.
📌 Must-Memorise

DMER → Medical Education + Tertiary Care

10. Directorate of Family Welfare

Its functions include:

  • Family welfare.
  • Reproductive-health programmes.
  • Demographic monitoring.
  • Maternal-child health indicators.

11. Three-Tier Health System

Tamil Nadu's public health-care system can broadly be classified as:

  • Primary care.
  • Secondary care.
  • Tertiary care.

12. Primary Health-Care Level

Primary care is delivered through:

  • Health Sub-Centres.
  • Primary Health Centres.
  • Urban primary-care facilities.

It emphasises prevention, screening and first-contact treatment.

13. Secondary Health-Care Level

Secondary care is mainly provided through:

  • Taluk hospitals.
  • Non-taluk hospitals.
  • District Headquarters Hospitals.

It handles cases requiring greater specialist and inpatient capacity.

14. Tertiary Health-Care Level

Tertiary care is provided mainly through:

  • Government Medical College Hospitals.
  • Super-speciality institutions.
  • Advanced diagnostic and surgical facilities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Primary → First Contact

Secondary → Specialist Hospital Care

Tertiary → Advanced/Super-Speciality Care

15. Ideal Referral Pathway

Community / HSC

→ PHC

→ Taluk or District Hospital

→ Medical College / Speciality Hospital

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Every Patient Need Not Begin at a Tertiary Hospital

16. Health Sub-Centre — Population Norm

According to the supplied source, a Health Sub-Centre generally covers:

  • Plain areas → 5,000 population.
  • Hilly/difficult areas → 3,000 population.
📌 Must-Memorise

HSC → 5,000 Plain / 3,000 Hilly-Difficult

17. Village Health Nurse

Village Health Nurses are important for:

  • Antenatal registration.
  • Maternal-child health.
  • Immunisation.
  • Family-planning counselling.
  • Community follow-up.

18. Health Inspector

Health Inspectors support:

  • Disease surveillance.
  • Health education.
  • Sanitation.
  • Birth and death registration.
  • Malaria and communicable-disease control.

19. Importance of Health Sub-Centres

  • HSCs represent the most peripheral institutional level of rural public health.
  • They bring preventive and maternal-child services close to communities.
📌 Must-Memorise

HSC → Health System at Community Level

20. Primary Health Centres — Core Functions

PHCs provide:

  • Outpatient treatment.
  • Maternal care.
  • Child health.
  • Immunisation.
  • Family planning.
  • Communicable-disease control.
  • NCD screening.
  • Referral.

21. Preventive Role of PHCs

Important preventive activities include:

  • Blood-pressure screening.
  • Diabetes screening.
  • Antenatal monitoring.
  • Vaccination.
  • Tuberculosis detection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Early Detection → Fewer Complications → Lower Treatment Cost

22. PHC Referral Role

  • PHCs are not limited to treatment of minor illness.
  • They also identify patients requiring higher-level care and coordinate referral.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Primary Care ≠ Minor Treatment Alone

23. District Headquarters Hospitals

District hospitals provide:

  • Specialist consultation.
  • Surgery.
  • Obstetric care.
  • Emergency treatment.
  • Inpatient care.

24. Taluk Hospitals

  • Taluk hospitals form an intermediate level between PHCs and major district or tertiary hospitals.
  • They help decentralise secondary care.

25. Importance of Secondary Hospitals

A strong secondary network reduces unnecessary crowding in medical college hospitals.

📌 Must-Memorise

PHC → Taluk/District → Tertiary Only When Needed

26. Government Medical College Hospitals

Medical college hospitals provide:

  • Advanced diagnosis.
  • Intensive care.
  • Specialist treatment.
  • Surgery.
  • Super-speciality care.
  • Clinical teaching.

27. Medical Colleges — Source-Dated Figure

  • The supplied July 2026 State Planning Commission material identified 61 medical colleges in Tamil Nadu.
⚠️ Current-Fact Rule

Medical-college totals can change; quote the reference year.

28. Teaching Hospitals — Triple Role

Teaching hospitals perform:

  • Patient care.
  • Training of health professionals.
  • Clinical teaching and research.
📌 Must-Memorise

Medical College Hospital → Care + Education + Research

29. TNMSC — Full Form

TNMSC stands for:

Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation

📌 Must-Memorise

TNMSC → Public Drug Procurement and Distribution

30. TNMSC — Origin

According to the supplied source:

  • Incorporated → 1994.
  • Procurement, storage and distribution functions began → 1995.
📌 Must-Memorise

TNMSC → 1994 / 1995

31. TNMSC — Core Function

TNMSC seeks uninterrupted availability of essential medicines through:

  • Central procurement.
  • Storage.
  • Warehousing.
  • Distribution to government health facilities.

32. Why Centralised Drug Procurement Matters

Potential advantages include:

  • Economies of scale.
  • Quality standardisation.
  • Better inventory management.
  • Lower procurement costs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Central Procurement → Warehousing → Facility → Patient

33. Medicine Availability and Effective Access

  • Free health care is incomplete if medicines are unavailable.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hospital Access + No Medicines ≠ Effective Treatment Access

34. National Health Mission Tamil Nadu

NHM Tamil Nadu supports:

  • Reproductive and child health.
  • Communicable-disease control.
  • NCD programmes.
  • Mental health.
  • Emergency care.
  • Urban health.
  • Tribal health.
  • Health-system strengthening.

35. NHM Implementation Model

The broad implementation model is:

National Framework

  • State Health System
  • District-Level Implementation

36. Maternal and Child Health

Tamil Nadu's maternal-child health system includes:

  • Early pregnancy registration.
  • Antenatal care.
  • Institutional delivery.
  • Immunisation.
  • Newborn care.
  • Referral transport.

37. Immunisation

  • Tamil Nadu has a long history of vaccine delivery through its public-health network.
  • Routine immunisation remains a core responsibility of primary public-health services.

38. SRS 2023 Health Indicators

According to the supplied Directorate of Family Welfare figures:

  • IMR → 12 per 1,000 live births.
  • MMR → 35 per 100,000 live births.
  • Crude Birth Rate → 12 per 1,000 population.
📌 Must-Memorise

IMR → per 1,000

MMR → per 100,000

39. Family Welfare Programme

  • Tamil Nadu has implemented the National Family Welfare Programme since 1956 on a voluntary basis.

It includes:

  • Contraceptive services.
  • Counselling.
  • Postpartum family planning.
  • Sterilisation services.
  • Reproductive-health care.

40. Tamil Nadu TFR — SRS 2023

  • The supplied source reports Tamil Nadu's Total Fertility Rate at 1.3 in SRS 2023.
📌 Must-Memorise

TFR 1.3 → Advanced Demographic Transition

41. Low Fertility — Health-System Consequence

Low fertility and longer survival increase the importance of:

  • Geriatric care.
  • Chronic-disease management.
  • Long-term care.
  • Social and health support for older persons.

42. Epidemiological Transition

Tamil Nadu increasingly faces a combined burden of:

  • Maternal and child health needs.
  • Communicable diseases.
  • Non-communicable diseases.
  • Ageing-related illnesses.
📌 Must-Memorise

Health Transition → Infectious + NCD + Ageing Burden

43. Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam

  • Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam represents a shift towards doorstep screening and continuing management of chronic disease.
  • It focuses particularly on non-communicable diseases.

44. MTM — Main Conditions

Major conditions include:

  • Hypertension.
  • Diabetes.
  • Other chronic illnesses requiring regular follow-up.

The supplied NHM framework refers to community screening particularly among older adults and persons at risk.

45. Why Doorstep NCD Care Matters

Chronic patients need:

  • Regular medicines.
  • Monitoring.
  • Follow-up.

Doorstep care can reduce:

  • Travel costs.
  • Wage loss.
  • Hospital crowding.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hospital-Centred Care → Community-Based Continuous Care

46. Padham Padhukappom

  • Padham Padhukappom Thittam is Tamil Nadu's integrated diabetic-foot care initiative.
  • The State issued an implementation order in October 2024.
📌 Must-Memorise

Padham Padhukappom → Diabetic-Foot Prevention

47. Diabetic-Foot Care Logic

The programme seeks to prevent:

Diabetes

→ Foot Complication

→ Ulcer/Infection

→ Disability/Amputation

through early screening and treatment.

48. Diabetic-Foot Clinics

  • The supplied source states that in February 2025, diabetic-foot clinics were sanctioned in 21 Government Medical College Hospitals.
⚠️ Current-Fact Rule

Quote the year with this figure.

49. 108 Emergency Response

  • Tamil Nadu's 108 Emergency Response system has operated since 15 September 2008.
📌 Must-Memorise

108 Emergency Service → 15 September 2008

50. 108 — Main Uses

The system supports emergencies including:

  • Road accidents.
  • Pregnancy complications.
  • Medical emergencies.
  • Neonatal emergencies.

51. Golden Hour

  • The Golden Hour refers to the critical early period after serious trauma when rapid treatment can substantially affect survival.
📌 Must-Memorise

Trauma → Rapid Response → Better Survival

52. Innuyir Kappom — Nammai Kaakkum 48

  • The scheme was launched on 18 December 2021.
  • It facilitates emergency treatment during the first 48 hours after road accidents under the notified framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nammai Kaakkum 48 → Road Accident → First 48 Hours

53. Idhayam Kappom

  • Idhayam Kappom Thittam was inaugurated on 27 June 2023 at Malumichampatti Health Sub-Centre in Coimbatore district.
📌 Must-Memorise

Idhayam Kappom → Early Heart-Attack Management

54. STEMI Hub-and-Spoke Model

The cardiac emergency pathway is:

Symptoms

→ Early Assessment

→ Loading Dose

→ Ambulance

→ Cardiac Centre

  • Hub hospitals with catheterisation facilities are linked with spoke institutions.

55. CMCHIS

CMCHIS stands for:

Chief Minister's Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme

Its objectives include:

  • Financial protection.
  • Improved access to secondary and tertiary hospital treatment.
  • Reduction of catastrophic medical expenditure.

56. CMCHIS — Income Eligibility

  • According to the supplied source, the general eligibility framework as of August 2026 uses annual family income below ₹1.20 lakh.
⚠️ TNPSC Current-Fact Rule

Eligibility limits can change.

57. CMCHIS — Empanelled Hospitals

The scheme operates through eligible empanelled:

  • Government hospitals.
  • Private hospitals.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CMCHIS = Health Financing

Not the Entire Tamil Nadu Health System

58. Disease-Control and Mental-Health Programmes

Tamil Nadu's health system addresses:

  • Tuberculosis.
  • Dengue and malaria.
  • HIV/AIDS.
  • Cancer.
  • Diabetes.
  • Cardiovascular disease.
  • Blindness.
  • Mental health.
  • Dialysis.
  • Oral health.
  • Tobacco control.
📌 Must-Memorise

Modern Public Health → Communicable + NCD + Mental Health

59. Mental-Health Services

The supplied source identifies services including:

  • District Mental Health Programme.
  • State Mental Health Programme.
  • Tele-Mental Health.
  • MaNaM Thittam.
  • Emergency Care and Recovery Centres.

60. Human Resources and Digital Health

A functional system requires:

Hospital

  • Equipment
  • Medicines
  • Doctors
  • Nurses
  • Allied Health Personnel
  • Infrastructure alone is insufficient.

Tamil Nadu is also expanding digital systems.

According to the supplied source:

  • HMIS 3.0 implementation was sanctioned in July 2025.
  • HMIS stands for Health Management Information System.
  • Tamil Nadu also participates in digital-health architecture including ABHA-related systems.

Future challenges include:

  • NCDs.
  • Ageing.
  • Rural–urban specialist gaps.
  • Mental health.
  • Human-resource availability.
  • Climate-related disease risks.
  • Digital privacy and accessibility.

The required transition is:

Treatment → Prevention

Hospital → Community

Episode Care → Continuous Care

Paper Records → Integrated Digital Health

Maternal-Child Focus Alone → Life-Course Health Care

TNPSC Traps

  • Health System ≠ Hospital Treatment Alone
  • Every Patient Need Not Begin at a Tertiary Hospital
  • Primary Care ≠ Minor Treatment Alone
  • Hospital Access + No Medicines ≠ Effective Treatment Access
  • CMCHIS = Health Financing Not the Entire Tamil Nadu Health System

  • PHC main functions? → First-contact care, prevention, screening and referral.

  • Medical colleges in supplied July 2026 material? → 61.

  • Procurement/distribution operations began? → 1995.
  • TNMSC core function? → Central procurement and supply of essential medicines.
  • NHM model? → National framework + State system + district implementation.
  • Main maternal-child interventions? → Antenatal care, institutional delivery, immunisation and newborn care.
  • Tamil Nadu IMR, SRS 2023? → 12 per 1,000 live births.
  • MMR, SRS 2023? → 35 per 100,000 live births.
